grand_strategy.reading:
Somalia is a state whose survival is contracted out. The federal government in Mogadishu
holds a capital, and little else it can call its own; its army is trained and its air power
flown by foreigners, its soldiers' allowances are paid by Brussels and the AU when they are
paid at all, and its budget rests on an IMF programme and a diaspora. A dozen patrons each
buy a piece - Ankara the base, the oil and the space range, Cairo and Asmara a pact aimed at
Addis Ababa, Doha and Riyadh a bet against Abu Dhabi, Beijing a vote against Taipei and
Hargeisa, Washington an air campaign it will not fully fund - and none of them buys the state,
so the patrons' quarrels become Somali politics. Luttwak's logic bites twice. Abroad, the
manoeuvre is relational: Mogadishu has learnt to sit at the seams of its patrons (at El Alamein
on 4 October, then on the telephone to Abiy on the 5th), but the seams run through its own
territory. At home the logic is paradoxical: every step to centralise (the March 2026
amendments, one person one vote, the parallel Gedo administration) makes the federation
weaker, because Puntland, Jubaland and Southwest answer by leaving, and the second week of
October 2026 shows the bill - Hees to al-Shabaab, Balad Hawo to Jubaland, Qansax Dheere to
Laftagareen, troops massed against opposition leaders at home. Three signals that are not rows:
a report, not confirmed by either government, that Somalia will buy Pakistani JF-17 fighters
(14 Oct); a former US ambassador calling the government 'illegitimate' (13 Oct), which is not
Washington's position; and the gap between 1,091 Egyptian AUSSOM troops and the 'about 15,000'
that The National attributes to Egypt in Somalia, which would mean a bilateral deployment outside
AUSSOM that no one has yet documented. The decisive date is 31 December 2026: if UNSOS lapses,
AUSSOM's contributors go home and the patrons' bets are exposed; if the US relents or the Gulf
pays, the same patrons will have bought the next piece.
